extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners / attorneys admitted to practice before the USPTO and USPTO disciplinary counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements governing attorney/practitioner conduct before the USPTO, OED investigatory and disciplinary procedures, and factors considered when imposing sanctions (including exclusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to timely answer constitutes admission/default
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to timely file an answer will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in entry of default judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e). The decision draws permissible inferences and treats admitted allegations as the Court's findings of fact when a respondent does not answer. Procedural timelines (e.g., deadlines set by Notice of Hearing and Order) and service methods (certified mail, publication) affect when an answer is due.

rubrics_metrics.name: OED Director burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving any alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. § 11.49. In a default the respondent is deemed to have admitted the allegations, which the tribunal may accept as proved.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO authority and right to discipline practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO has exclusive authority to establish qualifications for practice before it and to suspend or exclude practitioners for incompetence, disreputability, or gross misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounded in 35 U.S.C. § 2(b)(2)(D) and 35 U.S.C. § 32; disciplinary hearings conducted under 37 C.F.R. part 11, subpart C, and APA section 7.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service by publication and response period
rubrics_metrics.description: When personal service by mail is unsuccessful, notice may be served by publication and the respondent has thirty (30) days from the date of publication of the second notice to file an answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. § 11.35(b). Example: Notices published in Official Gazette on two consecutive weeks establish the 30-day answer deadline; failure to respond within that period permits default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respondent must keep address of record current
rubrics_metrics.description: A registered practitioner must notify the OED Director of the postal address for the practitioner's office and provide written notice of any address change within 30 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. § 11.11(a). Failure to keep an accurate address can affect service and is an obligation of practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act with reasonable diligence and promptness
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. § 11.103. Examples of violation include failure to respond to Notices to File Missing Parts, failure to respond to Notices of Abandonment, and failure to mitigate consequences leading to abandonment of patent applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep client reasonably informed about status
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the client's matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3). Illustrations: forwarding Office notices to client, advising of filing fees being unpaid, informing clients of potential consequences and options to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promptly comply with reasonable client requests for information
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall promptly comply with reasonable requests for information from the client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(4). Examples: responding to phone calls, voicemails, emails from clients or successor counsel; failing to do so is misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain matters sufficiently for informed client decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall explain a matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(b). Examples: advising clients about consequences of failing to pay filing fees or to respond to USPTO notices, and explaining options for revival or petitioning for extensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposit advance fees/expenses into client trust account
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall deposit into a client trust account legal fees and expenses that have been paid in advance, to be withdrawn only as fees are earned or expenses incurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. § 11.115(c). Example: funds collected for USPTO filing fees must be held in trust until used to pay USPTO; failing to deposit into trust is a violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promptly notify and deliver funds/property to client
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon receiving funds or other property in which a client has an interest, a practitioner shall promptly notify the client and promptly deliver funds or property the client is entitled to receive, and, upon request, render a full accounting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. § 11.115(d). Applied where practitioner collected filing fees but did not remit to USPTO or immediately return funds when not used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect client's interests upon termination of representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon termination, a practitioner shall take steps reasonably practicable to protect a client's interests (reasonable notice, allow time to employ other counsel, surrender papers/property, refund unearned fees).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. § 11.116(d). Examples of violation: failing to return client files, failing to return unearned filing fees, not communicating with successor counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c). Examples: representing that funds were collected for USPTO fees while not forwarding fees; mischaracterizing the nature of an Office notice to a client.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to cooperate with OED investigations and lawful demands
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to cooperate with an OED investigation or knowingly failing to respond to a lawful demand or request for information from a disciplinary authority is misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b) and 37 C.F.R. § 11.22(f) (RFI authority). Example: failure to respond to certified Request for Information and Evidence and subsequent Lack of Response letter constitutes violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d). The decision explains that failing to cooperate with disciplinary investigations undermines the integrity of the disciplinary system and public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner oath to observe laws and rules governing USPTO practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Each attorney licensed to practice before USPTO must sign an oath or affirmation to observe laws and rules governing USPTO practice; violating those rules breaches that oath.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a basis for concluding that failure to adhere to USPTO Rules and cooperate in investigations violates duties to clients, public, and profession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent/mental state matters (negligent, knowing, intentional conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Misconduct may be characterized as negligent, knowing, or intentional; willful or knowing/intentional misconduct supports more severe sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision finds respondent's conduct was negligent, knowing, and intentional; intentional failure to protect clients or return funds supports exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual injury to clients aggravates sanction
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct that causes actual injury to clients (e.g., abandonment leading to application abandonment and lost patent term/value) is an aggravating consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: all applications went abandoned, possible shortened patent life and delays in commercialization; actual injury supports a significant sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prior disciplinary case law and examples in sanctioning
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO disciplinary decisions consider prior USPTO case law and analogous state disciplinary decisions when evaluating misconduct and appropriate sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision cites multiple prior USPTO proceedings (exclusions, suspensions) and state cases to justify exclusion for abandonment, misappropriation-like conduct, and failure to return funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factors to increase sanction
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors per ABA Standards § 9.22 include: prior disciplinary offense; dishonest or selfish motive; pattern of misconduct; multiple offenses; bad faith obstruction of the disciplinary proceeding; substantial experience in the practice of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision enumerates and applies these aggravating factors (e.g., prior warning letter, pattern across multiple clients, failure to cooperate) to justify exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors may reduce sanction (but can be weak)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitigating factors per ABA Standards § 9.32 (e.g., absence of prior disciplinary record) may justify reduction in discipline but may be given little weight depending on the misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision acknowledges absence of prior formal sanction but treats it as weak mitigation given the gravity and pattern of the misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b) factors in choosing sanction
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions are determined after analyzing the factors enumerated in 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b) together with ABA Standards and the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court states exclusion is appropriate after applying these regulatory and ABA standards to the facts (default admissions, aggravating/mitigating factors, injury).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and eligibility for reinstatement after exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: An excluded practitioner is ineligible to practice before the USPTO and may apply for reinstatement no earlier than five years from the effective date of exclusion, subject to compliance requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58 (responsibilities on suspension/exclusion) and 11.60(b) (reinstatement eligibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural requirement: certified mailing and proof of delivery matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of certified mail (return receipt requested) and proof of delivery or return affects service and notice; receipt signatures and USPS markings (Return to Sender, Unclaimed, Unable to Forward) are material facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision documents multiple certified mail attempts, returns, and delivery receipts; such facts support conclusions about notice, attempts to contact, and whether respondent received RFI/Lack of Response letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Default: admitted allegations become operative factual findings
rubrics_metrics.description: When a respondent defaults, the tribunal may treat the complaint allegations as admitted and adopt them as findings of fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites case precedent and applies the rule to accept the Complaint's allegations as the Court's findings of fact upon respondent's failure to answer.
